name: WebDiagnosis Site Audit
author: Nicolas Blandel

sections.description:
Find what’s actually wrong with your WordPress site, and know exactly what to fix.

WebDiagnosis Site Audit is the WordPress audit that tells you what to fix, not just another score or generic list of recommendations.

Run 170+ automated checks across 14 critical areas including SEO, security, performance, accessibility, WordPress configuration, eco-design, and more.

Every finding tells you what was detected, why it matters, how urgent it is, and how to fix it.

Stop auditing. Start fixing.

Most audit tools give you a score and leave you to figure out what it means.

WebDiagnosis turns 170+ checks into a clear, prioritized action plan.

  • 170+ checks across 14 themes
  • Clear severity: Blocker, Major, Minor
  • No false alarms: unverified checks are reported as “Not verifiable”
  • Actionable findings: every issue includes its impact and recommended fix
  • Practical guidance: know what needs to change, who can do it, and how difficult it is

Built to be trusted

A score can tell you that something is wrong. A diagnosis tells you what to do next.

WebDiagnosis never guesses when the required data cannot be verified, and never turns a minor recommendation into an emergency.

The result: less time interpreting reports, more time fixing what actually matters.

One plugin. A complete website diagnosis.

Audit the dimensions that matter to modern WordPress websites:

  • SEO & technical SEO
  • Security
  • Performance & Core Web Vitals
  • Accessibility
  • WordPress configuration
  • Eco-design & sustainability
  • And more

Automatic monitoring after each update

Once you enable it, WebDiagnosis checks your site automatically after each update of WordPress, your theme or a plugin, whether you make it yourself, through automatic updates or with a maintenance tool. It can also check your site every week or every month, even when nothing changes on it.

  • One check per series of updates, a few minutes after the last one
  • Only when something really changed: a failed update that was rolled back triggers nothing
  • A notice tells you what was found after each check, and what changed on the site
  • Disabled by default, with its own consent, in Settings > Automatic monitoring

Know what matters. Fix what matters.

Other audit tools tell you how your website scores.
WebDiagnosis tells you what’s wrong and what to fix first.

External Services

This plugin connects to an external service to perform website diagnostics.

The plugin sends technical data about the site, never its posts, pages, comments or user
accounts. This data is sent only once you have accepted data sharing, and you can withdraw that
consent at any time from the plugin settings. Every request the plugin makes is listed below,
including the few it makes on its own.

Service name: WebDiagnosis
Service URL: https://webdiagnosis.io/en/

What the service is used for:
The service analyzes the WordPress website configuration and provides a diagnostic report with recommendations about performance, security and best practices.

What data is sent when a diagnostic runs:

  • Site URL, WordPress version, language and main WordPress settings (debug mode, permalinks, file editing, automatic updates, XML-RPC)
  • Server details: PHP and database (MySQL or MariaDB) versions, PHP limits, disk space, database size, caching, cron and file permissions
  • Installed plugins and themes, with their versions and update status
  • Security settings: whether the security keys WordPress uses are valid and whether they come from the site’s code or from the database (never the keys themselves), whether an account named “admin” exists and its role (never its password or email address)
  • The latest entries of the PHP error log: error type, message, line, and file path relative to the site root
  • Names, sizes and paths of sensitive files found under the site root (backups, database dumps, private keys). Their content is never read nor sent
  • Integrity of the WordPress core files: the paths, relative to the site root, of core files that differ from the official version and of unknown PHP files in the core folders. To compare them, the plugin downloads the checksums of your WordPress version from WordPress.org, as WordPress does for its own updates. File contents are never sent
  • Paths, sizes and modification dates of PHP files found in the uploads folder. Their content is never sent
  • Findings of a scan of the active theme’s code: file path, line and a short code excerpt for each finding
  • Content statistics: number of images with or without alternative text, menu locations, presence of the default sample content
  • Database statistics: total size of the options loaded on every page, with the names and sizes of the ten largest (never their values), and the number of revisions, automatic drafts, items in the trash and spam comments (never their content)
  • Your answer, once given, to the question whether your site is aimed at visitors in the European Union, the European Economic Area or the United Kingdom (yes, no or “I don’t know”). The service uses it to decide whether the GDPR and ePrivacy consent checks apply to your site
  • How the diagnostic was started: from the plugin interface, the WP-CLI command, the REST endpoints, the Abilities API or the automatic monitoring. The service uses it only for its usage statistics
  • A random number generated for each diagnostic and kept on the site for one hour. During the diagnostic, the service calls the site back once, at /wp-json/webdiagnosis/v1/ownership, to check that the request really came from this site before running its security checks (login page, sensitive files). The site answers with a fingerprint of the service’s challenge, never with the number itself

When data is sent:

  • When a diagnostic is explicitly requested: from the plugin interface, from the WP-CLI command, or through the plugin’s authenticated REST endpoints or the WordPress Abilities API.
  • When automatic monitoring is enabled, and only then: it is disabled by default and needs its own consent, given in Settings > Automatic monitoring. In the cases you tick, a diagnostic runs and sends the same data as a diagnostic you request yourself: a few minutes after WordPress, the theme or a plugin is updated, a plugin is activated or the theme is changed, once for a whole series of updates and only if the installed versions really changed since the last diagnostic. And regularly, every week or every month, once that long has passed since the last diagnostic.
  • When a fatal PHP error occurs on the site, and only if data sharing is accepted: the error type and message, its file path relative to the site root, its line, the page URL, the time, and the PHP and WordPress versions, so that the site owner can be alerted. Errors that could not be sent at once are retried every hour.
  • Once a day, and only if you have linked the plugin to a WebDiagnosis account with its key: the site URL and that key, to keep the account status shown in the plugin up to date.
  • When you request help from an expert or send feedback from the plugin: your name, your email address and your message, so that the WebDiagnosis team can answer you.
  • When you accept data sharing, deactivate, reactivate or delete the plugin, and only if data sharing is accepted: the site URL, the plugin version and the event, so that the service knows whether the plugin is still in use.
  • When you set a finding of the report aside, or restore it, and only if data sharing is accepted: the check concerned, the affected item if any (as shown in the report), your reason (“intended on my site” or “the diagnostic is wrong”), and the note you wrote, if any. The service keeps them so that every report of the site leaves the finding out, and uses the “wrong” reports to correct its checks. Without a WebDiagnosis account, the service checks that the request comes from your site with the same one-hour random number as a diagnostic, by calling the site back once.
  • To show the alerts and news of the WebDiagnosis team at the top of the diagnostic page (a newly announced vulnerability, a maintenance), and only if data sharing is accepted: the plugin reads the news feed of the service at most once an hour, usually every six hours. The request carries no data about the site, not even its address, only the plugin’s name and version. Whether an entry concerns your site (its PHP, WordPress, plugin or theme version) is decided on the site itself, never by the service.

Links to the service:
* Privacy policy: https://webdiagnosis.io/en/privacy-policy/
* Terms of service: https://webdiagnosis.io/en/terms-of-service/
sections.installation:
1. Download and install WebDiagnosis Site Audit from the WordPress plugins directory.
  2. Activate the plugin through the Plugins screen in WordPress.
  3. Go to WebDiagnosis Site Audit in the WordPress admin menu to run your first diagnostic.
  4. Optionally, enable automatic monitoring in Settings > Automatic monitoring.
sections.faq:
Does this plugin slow down my site?

No. The analysis itself runs on the WebDiagnosis service, not on your server. Diagnostics run when you trigger them, or, if you enable automatic monitoring, after an update and at the interval you choose. The plugin adds no frontend scripts and does not affect your visitors’ page load times.

Does the plugin run diagnostics on its own?

Only if you enable automatic monitoring, which is disabled by default and asks for its own consent. It then runs a diagnostic a few minutes after an update, and regularly if you tick that option. Each automatic diagnostic counts towards the diagnostic quota, and a notice in your admin tells you what it found. You can disable it at any time in Settings > Automatic monitoring.

What data is collected?

The diagnostic uses technical data such as your WordPress and PHP versions, active plugins, theme information, and server configuration. No personal data or site content is transmitted.

Do I need a WebDiagnosis account?

No. The plugin works on its own: accept data sharing and run a diagnostic. No account or key is needed.

Why does a check sometimes say “Not verifiable”?

Because WebDiagnosis doesn’t guess. If a check cannot access the data it needs, it reports “Not verifiable” instead of raising a potentially false issue.

Why does a diagnostic of a local or staging site show fewer checks?

Most checks look at your site from the internet, as a visitor or a search engine does: its pages, HTTP headers, certificate and exposed files. When the WebDiagnosis service cannot reach your site (a local site, a staging site behind a password, an intranet or a firewall), only the checks the plugin runs from inside WordPress are carried out, fewer than a third of them. The report says so at the top. For a full diagnostic, run it on the live site.

Is this plugin affiliated with WordPress?

No. WebDiagnosis Site Audit is an independent plugin developed by WebDiagnosis. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by WordPress, the WordPress Foundation, or Automattic.
sections.changelog:
1.6.0

  • Diagnostic reading redesigned: each finding shows the affected items at a glance, and a table of contents makes it easier to move through the report
  • A finding can be ignored on your site, or reported as an error to the WebDiagnosis team
  • A diagnostic started from the plugin is no longer lost when you leave the page: it keeps running in the background, and its progress display has been redesigned
  • New checks added (integrity of the WordPress core files, sensitive files left on server, outdated jQuery on theme or plugins)
  • PHP, database and web server version checks now follow official support dates and security releases
  • Alerts and news from the WebDiagnosis team on the diagnostic page and in the dashboard widget, telling you at once whether your site is concerned

1.5.0

  • Improved diagnostic time
  • A passed check that cannot verify everything says so, now reads “Passed with a reservation” and explains what to check yourself
  • The plugin asks whether your site is aimed at visitors in the European Union, the European Economic Area or the United Kingdom. For a site that is not, the GDPR and ePrivacy consent checks are given for information, with no penalty
  • Regular and automatic monitoring is now available. The plugin checks the site a few minutes after WordPress, the theme or a plugin changes, once for a whole series of updates
  • A diagnostic of a site the service cannot reach (local, staging, firewall) now says so at the top of the report, with the number of checks that could not be carried out
  • New tests added (SPF/DMARC, link analysis, etc.) and some tests improved

1.4.0

  • Pages whose HTML is an empty shell built by JavaScript are listed in the report, with the content checks that could not be carried out on them, instead of those checks being reported as passed
  • When the site’s anti-bot protection (Cloudflare, for instance) blocks the diagnostic robot, the plugin says so and explains how to allow it, instead of reporting the site as unreachable
  • The diagnostic now covers several pages, chosen automatically to cover different types of page (home, contact, product page or article). The dashboard shows them above the summary and lets you filter the diagnostic on one of them. Settings > Analysed pages explains how they are chosen
  • Known vulnerabilities of the installed WordPress version, plugins and theme (parent theme included) are now checked against the Wordfence Intelligence database, with the version to install and the english details
  • Affected items look the same in every check: one row each, with the version or value, a severity badge, a detail line and the action to take when there is one

1.3.1

  • Diagnostics can now be run far more often: the WebDiagnosis service sets the waiting time between two of them (one hour to start with) and a maximum per 24 hours (five to start with), instead of one per day
  • When the diagnostic quota is reached, the plugin shows the exact time of the next possible diagnostic, and says when the 24-hour maximum is the reason, instead of announcing it for tomorrow
  • Deleting the plugin now removes all of its settings, including the automated-access log and settings, which were left behind
  • Several tests improved

1.3.0

  • New security checks: an exposed Git or Subversion repository, a readable .env or credentials file, a forgotten phpinfo page, and backups, database dumps or private keys left downloadable under the site root
  • New check on the PHP error log: warnings and fatal errors repeating on every page load are now reported, with the file and the line
  • New check on the theme: content IDs written directly in templates that point to a page or post since deleted
  • Several tests improved and wording fixed in the summary and in the report
  • WP-CLI: output and help are now in English by default, with a new --lang=fr option
  • The follow-up token received from the WebDiagnosis service is now checked before use
  • The External Services section of this readme now lists all the data sent and when

1.2.0

  • Added an optional automated-access surface (REST route, WP-CLI command, WordPress Abilities API) so an AI agent or an integration pipeline can request an audit
  • The .htaccess check now sends only a yes/no verdict, never the file’s content
  • Settings are now split into tabs, and data sharing can be accepted from there without having to run a diagnostic first
  • Fixed two diagnostic status messages that were not translatable

1.1.0

  • Fixed and improved several checks
  • Restored 56 checks that were silently skipped
  • Fixed how translatable strings are handled, so the plugin can be translated into any language
  • Strengthened the checks run before a release is published

1.0.0

  • Initial public release
  • 14 diagnostic themes, 170+ checks
  • Structured data validated against search engine requirements
  • Plain-language explanation and fix for every finding
  • Bilingual interface (English/French)
  • Expert assistance request and feedback form
  • Optional connected mode with the WebDiagnosis platform
